 1857:
Leaders and Followers
 
One of the first acts of the sepoys of Meerut, as we saw, was to rush to
Delhi and appeal to the old Mughal emperor to accept the leadership of the

Shah’s first reaction was one of horror and rejection. It was only when

defiance of normal court etiquette, that the old emperor, realising he had

Kanpur, the sepoys and the people of the town gave Nana Sahib, no choice

popular pressure around her to assume the leadership of the uprising. So
was Kunwar Singh, a local zamindar in Bihar. In Awadh, where the
displacement of the popular Nawab Wajid Ali Shah and the annexation of
the state were still very fresh in the memory of the people, the populace in
Lucknow celebrated the fall of British rule by hailing Birjis Qadr, the young
son of the Nawab, as their leader. Elsewhere, local leaders emerged, urging
peasants, zamindars and tribals to revolt. Shah Mal mobilised the villagers

The Salt March was notable for at least three reasons. First, it was this

his party represented all of India came under challenge from three parties:
